lessons.title: What Is a Salt? Classification and Types

quiz.prompt: A bag of CAN fertiliser was left open overnight in a school storeroom. Washing soda crystals were left on a laboratory bench, and table salt was kept in a kitchen store. Which description matches what learners observed the next morning?
choices: The fertiliser granules stayed dry, the washing soda became wet and sticky, and the table salt clumped together.
The fertiliser granules turned into a fine powder, the washing soda stayed unchanged, and the table salt developed a white crust.
All three substances clumped together and felt wet and sticky.
The fertiliser granules clumped and felt wet, the washing soda crystals shrank and had a white powdery crust, and the table salt looked unchanged.
quiz.rationale: The observations were: fertiliser clumped and wet, washing soda shrunk with a white powdery crust, and table salt unchanged. The other options mix up which substance did what.
quiz.placement: Predict: three labelled photographs/displays (CAN fertiliser, washing soda, table salt) and the Think–Pair–Share prediction

quiz.prompt: Which statement gives the definition of a salt that learners annotated on their observation tables?
choices: A salt is only the white substance we add to food, sodium chloride.
A salt is any white solid that dissolves in water.
A salt is a substance formed when a hydrogen atom in an acid is fully or partially replaced by a positive ion.
A salt is a substance formed when the hydroxide ion of a base is replaced by a hydrogen atom.
quiz.rationale: A salt forms when hydrogen in an acid is fully or partially replaced by a positive ion. The other options describe colour, solubility or table salt only, which do not define salts in general.
quiz.placement: Observe: structured observation table and the KICD definition card

quiz.prompt: Table salt, NaCl, is a salt. Which acid and which positive ion would form it, by replacing hydrogen in the acid?
choices: Hydrochloric acid, with the hydrogen replaced by Na⁺
Nitric acid, with the hydrogen replaced by Na⁺
Sulphuric acid, with the hydrogen replaced by Na⁺
Hydrochloric acid, with the hydrogen replaced by Cl⁻
quiz.rationale: NaCl comes from hydrochloric acid, HCl, where H is replaced by the positive ion Na⁺. Cl⁻ is a negative ion and cannot replace hydrogen in the definition. Sulphuric and nitric acids would give sulphates and nitrates.
quiz.placement: Observe: annotating the observation table to identify which acid and positive ion formed each sample

quiz.prompt: Sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃, is used in baking. How is it classified?
choices: A normal salt, because it contains no OH⁻ ion
A double salt, because its formula contains two different elements besides oxygen
A basic salt, because it contains sodium, which comes from a base
An acidic salt, because only part of the hydrogen in the acid has been replaced and one H remains
quiz.rationale: NaHCO₃ still contains one hydrogen from carbonic acid, so the hydrogen is only partially replaced. That makes it an acidic salt. Having no OH⁻ does not make a salt normal.
quiz.placement: Explain: 16-card sorting activity and the exit check on NaHCO₃

quiz.prompt: Potassium aluminium sulphate (alum), KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O, is used to clean water. Which type of salt is it, and why?
choices: A double salt, because it contains two different positive ions, K⁺ and Al³⁺
A basic salt, because it contains water of crystallisation
A normal salt, because it has only one formula
An acidic salt, because it contains sulphate ions
quiz.rationale: Alum has two different metal (positive) ions, potassium and aluminium, so it is a double salt. Having one formula, containing water or containing sulphate does not decide the class.
quiz.placement: Explain: 16-card sorting activity (double salt cards)

quiz.prompt: Table salt (NaCl), washing soda (Na₂CO₃) and the salt in CAN fertiliser (NH₄NO₃) are all normal salts. Yet overnight in the open they behaved differently. What does this tell us?
choices: Table salt must not be a real salt, because it did not change.
Being a normal salt means a salt will always stay unchanged in the open.
Classifying the salts as normal does not by itself explain the different behaviour, so we still need to investigate other properties of salts.
The fertiliser and the washing soda must be acidic salts, because they changed.
quiz.rationale: All three are normal salts but behaved differently, so classification alone does not explain the phenomenon. The class still needs to investigate other properties. This is the open question carried into the next lesson.
quiz.placement: Explain: closing discussion returning to the phenomenon after the card sort ('classification alone does NOT explain the phenomenon')

quiz.prompt: Learners are posting pink 'question' sticky notes on the Driving Question Board about the fertiliser, washing soda and table salt. Which note is a good phenomenon-linked question?
choices: I wonder what a salt is.
I wonder why the storeroom door is always locked.
I wonder why CAN fertiliser clumps and feels wet overnight but table salt does not.
I wonder how much a bag of fertiliser costs.
quiz.rationale: A strong DQB question refers directly to the puzzle of the three salts behaving differently. 'What is a salt' is too vague, and the cost of fertiliser or the storeroom door is unrelated to the phenomenon.
quiz.placement: DQB: posting pink question sticky notes on the Driving Question Board

quiz.prompt: A learner says, "Copper sulphate is a coloured solid, so it will not dissolve in water." Which is the best way to test this idea?
choices: Look at the colour of the solid again and decide
Keep the sample in the vial and compare it with the white salts
Add a small measured amount to 5 mL of water in a test tube, stir, and observe whether the solid disappears
Ask more classmates and go with the majority
quiz.rationale: A prediction is tested with a controlled experiment: a small measured amount in a measured volume of water, stirred and observed. Colour alone, or opinion, is not evidence of solubility.
quiz.placement: Predict: individual Predict column in the lab table, sharing with a partner and the show-of-hands poll

quiz.prompt: Before the experiment, the teacher shows learners how to add only one level spatula tip (about 0.1 g) of salt to 5 mL of water. Why is this important?
choices: Adding more salt makes every salt become insoluble
Only a tiny amount can ever dissolve in any water
A larger amount of salt would make the test tube break
Too much salt can go beyond the solubility limit, so a soluble salt may wrongly look insoluble
quiz.rationale: If too much salt is added, some solid is left over even for a soluble salt. This would give a wrong conclusion, so a small, equal amount is used for every tube.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher demonstration with the extra NaCl sample before the structured experiment

quiz.prompt: A group stirs calcium carbonate in 5 mL of distilled water ten times and leaves it for 2 minutes. The mixture is still cloudy. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Calcium carbonate is soluble but needs to be stirred for an hour
Calcium carbonate is insoluble; the cloudiness is solid still suspended in the water
Calcium carbonate has dissolved and made a cloudy solution
No conclusion is possible because the water was distilled
quiz.rationale: A soluble salt disappears to give a clear solution. A mixture that stays cloudy after stirring and standing shows that undissolved solid remains, so the salt is insoluble.
quiz.placement: Observe: groups record whether the CaCO₃ mixture stays cloudy after stirring and after 2 minutes

quiz.prompt: A learner writes the rule: "All carbonates are insoluble in water." Which result from the solubility experiment shows this rule is wrong?
choices: Calcium carbonate stayed cloudy in water
Sodium chloride dissolved in water
Sodium carbonate dissolved in water
Lead sulphate stayed as a solid in water
quiz.rationale: Sodium carbonate is a carbonate that dissolved. This shows carbonates are not all insoluble: most are insoluble, but sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates are soluble.
quiz.placement: Explain: pairs identify patterns in the class chart (carbonates highlighted) and draft solubility rules

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the solubility of sulphates in water is correct?
choices: All sulphates are soluble, including lead(II) sulphate
All sulphates are insoluble
Only coloured sulphates are soluble
Most sulphates are soluble, but lead(II) sulphate is an insoluble exception
quiz.rationale: The solubility rules state that most sulphates are soluble, with exceptions such as lead(II) sulphate and barium sulphate. Copper sulphate dissolves, but lead sulphate does not.
quiz.placement: Explain: reading card of standard solubility rules, comparing with learners' drafted rules

quiz.prompt: Which answer best explains, using evidence, why table salt dissolves in githeri water but calcium carbonate (limestone) does not?
choices: Calcium carbonate is a bigger lump than table salt
Both are white solids, so they should behave the same way
Githeri water only dissolves salts that are used in cooking
Sodium chloride is a chloride, and most chlorides are soluble; in the experiment it dissolved. Calcium carbonate is a carbonate, and most carbonates are insoluble; in the experiment it stayed cloudy.
quiz.rationale: A good answer links the salt type to the solubility rule and to the experimental result for each salt: NaCl dissolved and CaCO₃ stayed cloudy.
quiz.placement: Explain and DQB: two-sentence answer to the Lesson 1 question about table salt, githeri water and calcium carbonate

quiz.prompt: Ammonium nitrate (in CAN fertiliser) dissolves in liquid water. A bag of CAN was left open overnight in a dry storeroom and the granules became wet and sticky, though no liquid water was added. What does this tell us?
choices: Solubility in liquid water alone does not explain the clumping, so the question remains open
Solubility in liquid water fully explains the clumping, so there is nothing more to investigate
The fertiliser must have been rained on during the night
Ammonium nitrate must be insoluble, because no liquid water was present
quiz.rationale: The experiment shows ammonium nitrate is soluble in liquid water, but no liquid water was present in the storeroom. So the overnight clumping is still unexplained and needs further investigation.
quiz.placement: Model Building: adding the Solubility column and the dashed arrow 'Why does it clump if there is no liquid water?' on the NH₄NO₃ box

lessons.title: Preparing Soluble Salts I — Acid + Metal and Acid + Metal Oxide (Experiment 2a)

quiz.prompt: Zinc granules are added to dilute sulphuric acid in a conical flask. What will you observe?
choices: The solution turns blue and a white solid forms at once
Nothing happens because zinc is a solid
Bubbles of gas form on the zinc, which slowly dissolves
A black solid dissolves and the solution turns blue
quiz.rationale: Zinc reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to give zinc sulphate solution and hydrogen gas, so bubbles appear and the zinc dissolves. The blue colour belongs to the copper(II) oxide reaction, not zinc.
quiz.placement: Predict-Record card: Setup A (zinc granules with dilute sulphuric acid)

quiz.prompt: A learner collects a gas over water from the reaction of zinc with dilute sulphuric acid. She brings a burning splint to the mouth of the test tube and hears a squeaky 'pop'. Which gas is present?
choices: Oxygen
Hydrogen
Ammonia
Carbon dioxide
quiz.rationale: Hydrogen burns explosively with a squeaky pop when a burning splint is brought to it. Oxygen relights a glowing splint, and carbon dioxide puts the flame out.
quiz.placement: Experiment A: collecting hydrogen and doing the pop test

quiz.prompt: In the preparation of zinc sulphate, excess zinc granules are added to the dilute sulphuric acid until the reaction stops. Why is excess zinc used?
choices: To turn the solution blue so that it is easy to see
To make sure all the acid is used up, so the filtrate contains only zinc sulphate solution
To make the zinc sulphate insoluble so that it can be filtered
To make the reaction produce more hydrogen gas
quiz.rationale: Excess metal makes sure that all the acid reacts. The leftover zinc is then filtered off, which leaves a filtrate with no acid in it. Zinc sulphate stays dissolved and is soluble.
quiz.placement: Experiment A: adding excess zinc until the reaction stops, then filtering

quiz.prompt: Black copper(II) oxide powder is added to dilute sulphuric acid and the mixture is warmed gently and stirred. What do you observe?
choices: The solution stays colourless and a brown solid forms
Bubbles of hydrogen gas form and the black powder stays unchanged
The black powder turns white and a pop is heard
The black powder dissolves and the solution turns blue
quiz.rationale: Copper(II) oxide reacts with the acid to form copper sulphate solution, which is blue, and water. No gas is produced, so there are no bubbles and no pop.
quiz.placement: Experiment B: preparing copper sulphate from black CuO and dilute sulphuric acid

quiz.prompt: Which equation correctly represents the reaction of copper(II) oxide with dilute sulphuric acid?
choices: CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Cu(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) + O₂(g)
CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)
CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)
quiz.rationale: A metal oxide plus an acid gives a salt plus water. The equation is balanced: Cu 1=1, S 1=1, H 2=2 and O 5=5. Hydrogen gas is not made in this reaction, and the sulphate ion is SO₄²⁻, not SO₃²⁻.
quiz.placement: Step 2 (equation writing): Reaction B, CuO + H₂SO₄

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes how a salt such as zinc sulphate is formed from an acid?
choices: The hydrogen in the acid is replaced by a metal ion
The sulphate part of the acid is replaced by oxygen
The acid gains extra hydrogen atoms from the metal
The whole acid molecule is destroyed and only water remains
quiz.rationale: A salt forms when the hydrogen of an acid is fully or partly replaced by a positive ion, such as a metal ion or the ammonium ion. In H₂SO₄ the hydrogen is replaced by Zn²⁺ to give ZnSO₄.
quiz.placement: Step 2 (equation writing): identifying the acid, the metal and the salt product in each equation

quiz.prompt: A learner says: 'Calcium ammonium nitrate fertiliser clumped in the storeroom because it is a salt made from an acid.' Table salt and washing soda are also soluble salts made from acids, but they behaved differently in the same air. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Knowing how a salt is made does not explain the clumping, so we must investigate how each salt behaves with water in the air
The statement is correct, because all salts made from acids take in water from the air
The statement is wrong, because CAN is not made from an acid
The statement is correct, because soluble salts always absorb water from the air
quiz.rationale: Table salt, washing soda and CAN are all soluble salts made by acid reactions, yet they behave differently. How a salt is made therefore cannot explain the clumping, and the salts' own properties and the air must be investigated.
quiz.placement: Step 3 (phenomenon connection) and the Driving Question Board orange cards

quiz.prompt: Ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃) is the soluble salt in CAN fertiliser. Which pair of reactants could be used to make it, by the same type of acid reaction used in today's lesson?
choices: Hydrochloric acid and copper(II) oxide
Sodium chloride and water
Sulphuric acid and zinc metal
Nitric acid and ammonia solution (a base)
quiz.rationale: Ammonium nitrate contains the nitrate ion from nitric acid and the ammonium ion from ammonia. The hydrogen of nitric acid is replaced by the ammonium ion when the acid is neutralised by the base.
quiz.placement: Speech bubble on the CAN fertiliser bag in the cumulative class model

lessons.title: Preparing Soluble Salts II — Acid + Base and Acid + Carbonate/Hydrogen Carbonate

quiz.prompt: Before the experiment, a learner predicts what forms when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution. Which prediction follows the pattern 'acid + base' from Lesson 3?
choices: Sodium chloride, carbon dioxide and water
Sodium oxide and chlorine gas
Sodium chloride and hydrogen gas
Sodium chloride and water
quiz.rationale: An acid reacting with a base (neutralisation) gives a salt and water, so HCl + NaOH gives NaCl + H₂O. Hydrogen is made with acid + metal, and CO₂ only with carbonates.
quiz.placement: Think-Pair-Share predictions for Experiment 2b (HCl + NaOH)

quiz.prompt: In Part A, universal indicator is added to 25 cm³ of 1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Sodium hydroxide solution is then added a little at a time. The final mixture looks like clear water, with no bubbles and no solid. Which observation shows that neutralisation is complete?
choices: The indicator stays red, pH about 1
The indicator turns green, pH about 7
The mixture bubbles and gives off a gas
The indicator turns purple, pH about 14
quiz.rationale: Neutralisation gives no gas or precipitate, so the indicator colour is the evidence. The colour changes from red to orange, yellow and then green, and green (pH about 7) marks the endpoint.
quiz.placement: Part A: neutralisation (NaCl preparation) with universal indicator

quiz.prompt: In Part B, marble chips (calcium carbonate) are reacted with dilute hydrochloric acid. The gas produced bubbles through limewater, and the limewater turns milky. Which gas is present?
choices: Chlorine
Carbon dioxide
Hydrogen
Oxygen
quiz.rationale: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to form a white suspension, so the limewater turns milky. This is the standard test for CO₂, which is released when an acid reacts with a carbonate.
quiz.placement: Part B: acid + carbonate (CaCl₂ preparation) with CO₂ collection and limewater test

quiz.prompt: After the experiment, the used solutions have to be dealt with. Which is the correct way to handle the waste from Experiment 2b?
choices: Leave the waste open on the bench so it evaporates
Pour the waste into the school water tank
Pour the acid waste straight down the sink without any treatment
Neutralise the waste solutions first, then pour them down the sink
quiz.rationale: Acid or alkali waste must be neutralised before disposal so it does not harm people, pipes or the environment. This is the waste disposal procedure used at clean-up.
quiz.placement: Clean-up: waste disposal procedure after Parts A and B

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct balanced equation for hydrochloric acid reacting with calcium carbonate?
choices: 2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O
2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂ + H₂O
2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl + CO₂ + H₂O
HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O
quiz.rationale: CaCl₂ needs 2 Cl atoms, so 2HCl is needed. Both sides then have 1 Ca, 2 Cl, 2 H, 1 C and 3 O. The first option has unbalanced Cl and H, the second has the wrong formula for calcium chloride, and the third has no carbon dioxide.
quiz.placement: Word Equation → Balanced Equation scaffold: Reaction B (HCl + CaCO₃)

quiz.prompt: In mandazi dough, baking soda (sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃) reacts with an acid in the dough and the dough rises. What are the products of this type of reaction?
choices: A salt, water and oxygen
A salt and hydrogen gas only
A salt, water and carbon dioxide
A salt and water only
quiz.rationale: An acid reacting with a carbonate or hydrogen carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide. The CO₂ bubbles make the mandazi dough rise, as in HCl + NaHCO₃ → NaCl + CO₂ + H₂O.
quiz.placement: Phenomenon Connection box: mandazi dough and NaHCO₃

quiz.prompt: A group makes a mini flow chart for two methods: acid + base and acid + carbonate. Which statement correctly compares the two methods?
choices: Only acid + base makes water, and only acid + carbonate makes a salt
Neither method makes water, but both make a salt
Both make a salt and water, but only acid + carbonate also makes carbon dioxide
Both make a salt, water and carbon dioxide
quiz.rationale: Acid + base gives salt + water. Acid + carbonate gives salt + water + CO₂ gas. Both methods make a salt and water, and only the carbonate method also makes carbon dioxide.
quiz.placement: Mini flow chart cards for acid + base and acid + carbonate, posted in the 'Experiment 2b Evidence' section

quiz.prompt: A learner adds the final two branches to the cumulative flow chart of soluble salt preparation methods. Which branch is written correctly?
choices: Acid + Carbonate → Salt + Water only
Acid + Carbonate/Hydrogen carbonate → Salt + CO₂ + Water
Acid + Base → Salt + CO₂ + Water
Acid + Base → Salt + Hydrogen
quiz.rationale: Acid + carbonate or hydrogen carbonate gives a salt, CO₂ and water. Acid + base gives only a salt and water, with no gas.
quiz.placement: Cumulative 'Soluble Salt Preparation Methods' flow chart: adding branches (3) and (4)

lessons.title: Preparing Insoluble Salts — Double Decomposition and Precipitation

quiz.prompt: A teacher pours barium chloride solution (0.1 mol/L) into sodium sulphate solution (0.1 mol/L). Both solutions are clear and colourless. What will you see?
choices: The mixture fizzes as a gas is given off
A white solid forms immediately
A golden-yellow solid forms immediately
The mixture stays clear because both salts are dissolved in water
quiz.rationale: Barium sulphate is one of the insoluble sulphate exceptions, so Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions join to form a white precipitate as soon as the solutions mix.
quiz.placement: Predict: Beaker A (barium chloride) poured into Beaker B (sodium sulphate) and learners' written predictions

quiz.prompt: After mixing barium chloride and sodium sulphate solutions, a group filters the mixture. Which is the correct way to treat the two parts?
choices: Keep the white residue on the filter paper as the product and collect the filtrate in a labelled waste beaker
Keep the white residue on the filter paper as the product and pour the filtrate down the sink
Collect both the residue and the filtrate in the waste beaker, because neither is useful
Keep the filtrate as the product and throw away the white residue
quiz.rationale: The precipitate (residue) is the insoluble salt that was made. The filtrate is waste and must be collected, not poured down the sink, because barium ions are toxic to aquatic life.
quiz.placement: Primary experiment (barium sulphate): filtering, washing and collecting filtrate in the labelled waste beaker

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct balanced equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between barium chloride solution and sodium sulphate solution?
choices: BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + NaCl₂(aq)
BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + NaCl(aq)
BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(aq) + 2NaCl(s)
quiz.rationale: Two Na and two Cl are needed on the right, so the coefficient of NaCl is 2. BaSO₄ is the insoluble precipitate (s) and NaCl stays dissolved (aq).
quiz.placement: Layer 1 — Word and symbol equations (balanced molecular equation on mini-whiteboards)

quiz.prompt: Barium chloride solution reacts with sodium sulphate solution to form a precipitate of barium sulphate. The Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are spectator ions. What is the net ionic equation?
choices: Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → NaCl(s)
BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
2Na⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → Na₂SO₄(s)
Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)
quiz.rationale: Only the ions that join to form the precipitate appear in the net ionic equation: Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ form BaSO₄(s). Na⁺ and Cl⁻ stay in solution unchanged, so they are cancelled.
quiz.placement: Layer 2 — Ionic equations: Think-Aloud on spectator ions and the net ionic equation

quiz.prompt: Lead(II) nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution and a golden-yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide forms. Which ions are the spectator ions?
choices: K⁺ and NO₃⁻
K⁺ and I⁻
Pb²⁺ and NO₃⁻
Pb²⁺ and I⁻
quiz.rationale: Pb²⁺ and I⁻ combine to form the PbI₂ precipitate. K⁺ and NO₃⁻ stay dissolved and unchanged on both sides, so they are the spectator ions.
quiz.placement: Alternative experiment (lead(II) iodide) and Layer 2 — spectator ions

quiz.prompt: Which of these salts must be prepared by double decomposition (precipitation) rather than by dissolving a metal, base or carbonate in an acid?
choices: Barium sulphate, which is insoluble
Ammonium nitrate, which is soluble
Potassium nitrate, which is soluble
Sodium chloride, which is soluble
quiz.rationale: Insoluble salts are made by mixing two soluble salt solutions so that the insoluble product precipitates. The other three salts are soluble and can be made by neutralisation.
quiz.placement: Layer 3 — Method Comparison Chart (Precipitation / Double Decomposition column)

quiz.prompt: A learner asks: "Why can't we make barium sulphate by reacting barium metal with sulphuric acid in the lab?" Which answer is correct?
choices: Barium sulphate is soluble, so it would dissolve and could not be collected
The reaction would be violently exothermic and dangerous, and insoluble barium sulphate would coat the metal and stop the reaction
Sulphuric acid cannot react with any metal
Barium is a very unreactive metal, so no reaction takes place
quiz.rationale: Barium is a reactive Group 2 metal, so the reaction is violent. The insoluble BaSO₄ formed also coats the metal and stops the reaction.
quiz.placement: Layer 3 — key question: 'Why can't we make barium sulphate by reacting barium metal with sulphuric acid directly in the lab?'

quiz.prompt: Barium ions are toxic, yet patients at hospitals such as Kenyatta National Hospital swallow barium sulphate in a "barium meal" before stomach X-rays. Why is this safe?
choices: Barium ions are toxic only when they are in a solid
Barium sulphate is soluble, and the body quickly breaks it down into harmless substances
The barium sulphate is mixed with sodium chloride, which cancels the toxic effect
Barium sulphate is insoluble, so it cannot dissolve and be absorbed into the bloodstream
quiz.rationale: Because BaSO₄ is insoluble, it does not release barium ions into the blood. The same property that means it must be made by precipitation also makes it safe in medicine.
quiz.placement: Model Building: 'Kenyan context' annotation on the insoluble-salts branch (barium meal at Kenyatta National Hospital)

lessons.title: Behaviour of Salts in Air: Hygroscopic, Deliquescent and Efflorescent Salts

quiz.prompt: In Experiment 3, a group weighs a watch glass of anhydrous calcium chloride (CaCl₂) at 2.00 g at the start. After 25 minutes in open classroom air it reads 2.46 g. What is the mass change, Δm = final − initial?
quiz.rationale: Δm = final − initial = 2.46 − 2.00 = +0.46 g. The positive sign shows the sample gained mass by absorbing water vapour from the air.
quiz.placement: Experiment 3: recording Time 0 and final mass, then calculating Δm for each sample

quiz.prompt: A group weighs 2.00 g of sodium chloride (NaCl) on a watch glass and leaves it open for 25 minutes in a normal classroom. The final reading is 2.01 g and the crystals look unchanged. What is the best conclusion?
choices: There was no significant change, because a difference of 0.01 g is within balance error at everyday humidity
NaCl is efflorescent because its crystals stayed dry
NaCl is deliquescent because its mass increased
NaCl lost its water of crystallisation to the air
quiz.rationale: A 0.01 g difference is within balance error, so NaCl showed no real change. NaCl takes up water only when the air is very humid (above about 75% relative humidity).
quiz.placement: Experiment 3: class data table comparing Sample C (NaCl) across groups

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a deliquescent salt?
choices: It absorbs water vapour from the air until it dissolves in the water it has absorbed
It absorbs some water from the air but never dissolves in it
It does not interact with water vapour in the air at all
It loses water of crystallisation to the air and turns into a powder
quiz.rationale: A deliquescent salt such as CaCl₂ absorbs so much water vapour that it dissolves in it. Absorbing water without dissolving describes a hygroscopic salt, and losing water describes an efflorescent salt.
quiz.placement: Frayer Model: defining hygroscopic, deliquescent and efflorescent using experimental data

quiz.prompt: Washing soda crystals (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) left in open air lose water of crystallisation and form a white powder of the monohydrate, Na₂CO₃·H₂O. Which is the correct balanced equation for this efflorescence?
choices: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O(s) → Na₂CO₃·H₂O(s) + 10H₂O(g)
Na₂CO₃·10H₂O(s) → Na₂CO₃·H₂O(s) + 9H₂O(g)
Na₂CO₃·10H₂O(s) + 9H₂O(g) → Na₂CO₃·H₂O(s)
Na₂CO₃·10H₂O(s) → Na₂CO₃·H₂O(s) + 8H₂O(g)
quiz.rationale: The crystal has 10 water molecules and the product keeps 1, so 9 H₂O escape as vapour. The other options are unbalanced or show water being gained.
quiz.placement: Writing the balanced equation for efflorescence with state symbols on the worksheet

quiz.prompt: A bag of CAN fertiliser (calcium ammonium nitrate) is left open overnight in a storeroom. The granules clump together and feel wet and sticky, although no water was added. What is the best explanation?
choices: The ammonium nitrate in CAN absorbed water vapour from the air and dissolved in it, like a deliquescent salt
The ammonium nitrate in CAN is efflorescent and lost water of crystallisation to the air
The limestone in CAN absorbed water from the air and made the granules stick together
The CAN is unchanged like table salt, and the wetness came from the bag
quiz.rationale: The ammonium nitrate in CAN takes in water vapour from the air and dissolves in it, which is deliquescence. The limestone in CAN does not take up water.
quiz.placement: Matching each sample to the anchoring phenomenon: 'Sample A = CAN fertiliser because...'

quiz.prompt: A learner writes the answer to the driving question on a green card. Which storage advice for Kenyan farms and laboratories is correct?
choices: Sealed containers are only needed for table salt, because it is the salt that changes most in air
Store CAN fertiliser in open bags, because deliquescent salts need air to stay dry
Store CAN fertiliser in sealed, airtight bags and washing soda in sealed containers
Keep washing soda in an open dish so its crystals can take in water
quiz.rationale: CAN is deliquescent, so it must be sealed from moist air to prevent clumping. Washing soda is efflorescent, so it must be sealed to keep its water of crystallisation. NaCl is stable at everyday humidity.
quiz.placement: Green card: first complete answer to the driving question, including a storage recommendation

quiz.prompt: A learner draws a particle diagram for efflorescent washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) left in open air. Which drawing of the water molecules is scientifically correct?
choices: Arrows point away from the crystal into the air, showing separate water molecules leaving the lattice
Arrows point away from the crystal, but the water is drawn as a continuous liquid layer
No arrows, because the water molecules stay still inside the crystal
Arrows point into the crystal, because water molecules are attracted from the air
quiz.rationale: In efflorescence, water molecules leave the crystal lattice and escape into the air as separate particles. This leaves the white powdery residue. Inward arrows would show deliquescent behaviour.
quiz.placement: Cumulative particle model: Panel 6, side-by-side diagram of deliquescent, efflorescent and stable salt surfaces

lessons.title: Applications of Salts in Daily Life in Kenya

quiz.prompt: Granules of CAN fertiliser were left in an open bag in a school storeroom overnight. By morning they had clumped together and felt wet and sticky, although no water was added. Which property of CAN explains why Rift Valley farmers must store it in sealed bags?
choices: It loses its water of crystallisation to the air (it is efflorescent)
It evaporates slowly when left in the open
It reacts with oxygen in the air to form a sticky oil
It absorbs so much water vapour from the air that it becomes wet (it is deliquescent)
quiz.rationale: CAN takes in water vapour from humid air and becomes wet and clumped, so it must be kept sealed. Loss of water of crystallisation (efflorescence) would produce a dry powder, not a sticky mass.
quiz.placement: Predict: image A, the Rift Valley maize farmer pouring CAN fertiliser (property of the salt and link to earlier lessons)

quiz.prompt: Heavy rain washes extra inorganic fertiliser (nitrates and phosphates) from maize farms into rivers that flow into Lake Victoria. What is a likely effect on the lake?
choices: Fish numbers increase because the water has fewer plants
The lake water becomes more acidic because sodium chloride is added
Algal blooms and water hyacinth grow rapidly
The water becomes harder because calcium carbonate dissolves
quiz.rationale: Nitrates and phosphates are plant nutrients. When they run into the lake they feed algal blooms and water hyacinth, which harm the lake and its fish.
quiz.placement: Observe: Expert Group 1 (Agriculture), effects of too much inorganic fertiliser and ways to reduce them

quiz.prompt: Which action would best reduce the harm that excess inorganic fertiliser does to rivers and soil?
choices: Stop using manure and compost and use only inorganic fertiliser
Spread the fertiliser on bare, sloping ground so the rain can wash it in
Apply only the recommended amount at the right time, and also use manure and compost
Apply double the amount before the rains so the crop always has enough
quiz.rationale: Using only the recommended amount at the right time, and adding manure and compost, means less fertiliser is left to be washed into rivers. Planting along the contours also helps.
quiz.placement: Observe: Expert Group 1 (Agriculture), ways to reduce the effects of too much fertiliser

quiz.prompt: Fishmongers at Dunga Beach on Lake Victoria rub sodium chloride onto fresh tilapia to preserve it. Which statement best explains why this works?
choices: Every salt is poisonous to bacteria, so any salt would preserve the fish equally well
The salt reacts with the fish to make carbon dioxide, which kills bacteria
The salt draws water out of the fish and out of microbes, so bacteria cannot grow well
The salt is deliquescent, so it makes the fish wetter and keeps it fresh
quiz.rationale: Sodium chloride dissolves in the water on the fish and draws water out (an osmotic effect). Without water, bacteria cannot grow. Not all salts preserve food, so the claim that any salt works is a misconception.
quiz.placement: Observe: Expert Group 2 (Food Industry), sodium chloride for preserving omena and tilapia

quiz.prompt: A child with diarrhoea loses water and dissolved ions from the body. A nurse at a rural dispensary mixes oral rehydration salts (ORS) in water for the child. Which salts in ORS help to replace the lost ions?
choices: Barium sulphate and titanium dioxide
Ammonium sulphate and single super phosphate
Sodium carbonate and calcium carbonate
Sodium chloride and potassium chloride (with sodium citrate)
quiz.rationale: ORS contains sodium chloride, potassium chloride and sodium citrate, with glucose, to replace the sodium and potassium ions and water lost in diarrhoea. The other choices are pigments, glass or laundry salts, and fertilisers.
quiz.placement: Observe: Expert Group 3 (Medicine), oral rehydration salts and why ionic composition matters

quiz.prompt: Barium sulphate is used as a white pigment in paint. Which property makes it suitable for this use?
choices: It is very soluble in water, so it spreads evenly through the wall
It is efflorescent, so it forms a powdery layer on the wall
It is deliquescent, so it keeps the paint wet
It is insoluble in water, so it stays as a solid and does not dissolve or wash away
quiz.rationale: Barium sulphate is insoluble in water, according to the solubility rules. It therefore stays as a white solid pigment in the paint and does not dissolve or wash off.
quiz.placement: Observe: Expert Group 4 (Paper and Paint Industries), barium sulphate as a white pigment and the insolubility rule

quiz.prompt: Soda ash (sodium carbonate) from Lake Magadi is added to sand (silica) when glass is made. What is its main job?
choices: It raises the melting point so the glass is stronger
It softens the glass so that it never breaks
It acts as a flux that lowers the melting point of the silica
It makes the glass white by acting as a pigment
quiz.rationale: Silica melts at a very high temperature. Sodium carbonate is a flux: it lowers the melting point, which saves energy and makes glass-making easier.
quiz.placement: Observe: Expert Group 5 (Glass Industry), sodium carbonate (soda ash) as a flux

quiz.prompt: Washing soda (sodium carbonate) softens hard water in laundry. Which statement explains how?
choices: Carbonate ions react with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions in the water to form insoluble CaCO₃ and MgCO₃, which are removed as solids
Washing soda adds more calcium and magnesium ions, so the soap lathers better
Sodium ions in washing soda dissolve the calcium and magnesium ions in the water
The washing soda crystals lose water and absorb the calcium and magnesium ions as gases
quiz.rationale: Carbonate ions combine with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ to form insoluble carbonates, which precipitate out. This is the same kind of precipitation reaction studied earlier. Once these ions are removed, the water is soft.
quiz.placement: Observe: Expert Group 6 (Laundry Industry), washing soda as a water softener and the precipitation link to Lesson 5

quiz.prompt: A container of washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) left open on a laboratory bench developed a white powdery crust and the crystals looked smaller. Which statement correctly explains this, and what does it mean for storage?
choices: It is efflorescent: it loses water of crystallisation to the air, so it should be kept in a closed container
It is hygroscopic and gains mass, so it should be kept in the sun
It is deliquescent: it absorbs water from the air and dissolves, so it should be kept open to dry
It is insoluble, so it reacts with oxygen to form the crust
quiz.rationale: Washing soda is a hydrated salt that loses some of its water of crystallisation to the air. This leaves a white powdery crust and makes the crystals shrink. A closed container keeps the crystals from changing. This is a separate property from deliquescence in CAN.
quiz.placement: Explain: Whole-Class Synthesis using the Property → Use → Phenomenon framework (washing soda)

quiz.prompt: Table salt (NaCl) in a kitchen store was left open in ordinary air and looked completely unchanged, unlike CAN fertiliser and washing soda. Which statement best explains this?
choices: It is insoluble in water, so it never changes
It neither absorbs enough water from ordinary air to become wet nor loses water of crystallisation, so it can be stored open
It is deliquescent, so it always becomes a clear solution overnight
It is not a salt, so air has no effect on it
quiz.rationale: Table salt is neither deliquescent nor efflorescent in ordinary air, and it has no water of crystallisation to lose. It therefore stays unchanged, unlike CAN, which absorbs water, and washing soda, which loses water.
quiz.placement: Explain: Whole-Class Synthesis using the Property → Use → Phenomenon framework (table salt)

lessons.title: Unit Synthesis, Model Revision and Summative Assessment

quiz.prompt: A container of washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) is left on a laboratory bench. After a few days it has a white powdery crust and the crystals look smaller. What is the correct scientific term for this change?
choices: Precipitation, because a new solid forms in solution
Hygroscopy, because the crystals take in water without dissolving
Efflorescence, because the crystals lose water of crystallisation to the air
Deliquescence, because the crystals absorb water and dissolve
quiz.rationale: Washing soda loses some of its water of crystallisation to the air (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O → Na₂CO₃·H₂O + 9H₂O). This leaves a powdery crust and shrunken crystals, which is efflorescence.
quiz.placement: Return to Phenomenon: writing the 'What I can now explain' card (washing soda crust and shrunken crystals)

quiz.prompt: Table salt (NaCl) kept in an ordinary kitchen store stays dry and unchanged for months, while CAN fertiliser left open becomes wet and sticky. Which explanation for the table salt is correct?
choices: NaCl is insoluble in water, so it can never take in moisture
NaCl takes up water from the air only when the air is very humid (above about 75% relative humidity), so it is unchanged at everyday humidity
NaCl contains water of crystallisation, which keeps it from changing
NaCl is not a salt, so it does not behave like the other two substances
quiz.rationale: NaCl only absorbs water vapour when relative humidity is very high (above about 75%). At ordinary storeroom humidity it stays unchanged, unlike CAN, which absorbs water more readily.
quiz.placement: Return to Phenomenon: writing the 'What I can now explain' card (why table salt was unchanged)

quiz.prompt: A group's preparation-pathway flowchart on the poster includes precipitation. Which of these salts would be prepared by precipitation, by mixing two soluble salt solutions?
choices: Potassium nitrate
Ammonium sulphate
Lead(II) sulphate
Sodium chloride
quiz.rationale: Precipitation is used for insoluble salts. Lead sulphate is an exception among the sulphates, so it forms as a solid when, for example, lead nitrate and sodium sulphate solutions are mixed. The other three salts are soluble.
quiz.placement: Comparative Model Gallery Walk: checking the solubility rules and preparation pathway flowchart on the final cumulative model

quiz.prompt: A Kenyan agrochemical company makes salt X by reacting sulphuric acid with ammonia solution until the acid is completely neutralised. Salt X is ammonium sulphate, (NH₄)₂SO₄. How is ammonium sulphate classified?
choices: Acidic salt
Double salt
Normal salt
Basic salt
quiz.rationale: All the replaceable hydrogen ions of the acid have been replaced by NH₄⁺ ions. The salt has no leftover H⁺ or OH⁻, so it is a normal salt.
quiz.placement: Summative task part (a): name salt X and classify it

quiz.prompt: Sulphuric acid reacts with ammonia solution to make ammonium sulphate. Which balanced equation shows this reaction?
choices: H₂SO₄ + 2NH₃ → (NH₄)₂SO₄
H₂SO₄ + NH₃ → NH₄SO₄
H₂SO₄ + 2NH₃ → (NH₄)₂SO₄ + H₂
H₂SO₄ + NH₃ → (NH₄)₂SO₄
quiz.rationale: Each H₂SO₄ gives two H⁺ ions, so it needs two NH₃ molecules to form two NH₄⁺ ions. This gives H₂SO₄ + 2NH₃ → (NH₄)₂SO₄ with N, H, S and O balanced. The reaction is not metal + acid, so no hydrogen gas forms.
quiz.placement: Summative task part (b): write a balanced equation for the preparation of salt X

quiz.prompt: Ammonium sulphate fertiliser takes up water vapour only when the air is very humid (above about 80% relative humidity). It is stored in an open warehouse near Lake Nakuru. Which statement is correct?
choices: It is unchanged in all weather because it is a salt, so no special storage is needed
On an ordinary dry day it loses water of crystallisation and forms a powdery crust, so it should be kept in open sacks
On a very humid, rainy night it is hygroscopic and may become damp and clump; on an ordinary dry day it stays dry; it should be kept in sealed bags
On an ordinary dry day it absorbs so much water that it dissolves completely, so it should be kept in the sun
quiz.rationale: The salt absorbs water only at high humidity, so it is hygroscopic. It may get damp and clump on a humid night but stays dry on a dry day. Sealed bags protect it from moist air.
quiz.placement: Summative task part (c): explain what happens to stored salt X on a very humid night and on an ordinary dry day, and how it should be stored

quiz.prompt: Which pairing of a salt with a correct Kenyan use is right?
choices: Sodium chloride: preserving and drying fish such as omena and tilapia at Lake Victoria
Washing soda: fertiliser for maize farms in the Rift Valley
Sodium chloride: fertiliser for maize farms in the Rift Valley
Calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN): preserving fish at Lake Victoria
quiz.rationale: Sodium chloride is used to preserve and dry fish such as omena and tilapia. CAN is a fertiliser for maize farms, and washing soda is used for laundry.
quiz.placement: Model Evolution Share: Kenyan applications panel on the final cumulative model
